lessons.unit: Unit 2: Fables - reading and writing a story with a moral
lessons.title: Reading a fable: The Hare and the Tortoise
objectives: Describe the features of a fable
Retrieve and explain information from a short text

keywords.def: a short story with animal characters that teaches a lesson
the lesson a story teaches
a person or animal in a story
find information in a text

starter: Bismillah. Name one conjunction and use it in a sentence.
What does the prefix mis- mean?
Write an expanded noun phrase about a river.

teach.heading: What is a fable?
bullets: A short story with a lesson
A fable ends with a moral
Aesop is the best-known writer of fables
teach.note: Introduce fables as very old stories told to teach good behaviour. Ask pupils which stories with animals they know. Explain that the animals have one main quality, such as pride or kindness.

teach.heading: Read the fable
bullets: The hare boasts about his speed
They race to the oak tree
The hare naps; the tortoise keeps going
teach.note: Aesop's fable, retold: A hare laughed at a tortoise for being so slow. 'I could win any race with my eyes closed,' he boasted. 'Then let us race,' said the tortoise quietly. A fox marked the finish line at the old oak tree. 'Ready, steady, go!' The hare shot off and was soon far ahead. Looking back, he saw that the tortoise had hardly moved. 'I have plenty of time,' he yawned, and lay down under a tree for a nap. The tortoise plodded on, step by step, and never stopped. When the hare woke, the sun was low. He sprinted towards the oak tree, but the tortoise was already crossing the line. Moral: slow and steady wins the race. Read aloud with expression. Pause after the boast and ask pupils to predict what will happen.

teach.heading: Find the facts
bullets: Quote the text to prove it
teach.note: Model retrieval: find a sentence that answers 'Who marked the finish line?' Show how to scan for key words and underline the answer. Remind pupils to answer in a sentence.

teach.heading: Why did the tortoise win?
bullets: Boasting led to the hare's mistake
teach.note: Ask for answers starting 'The tortoise won because...'. Accept reasons from the text: the hare slept. Model a full sentence answer.

teach.heading: The moral
bullets: Slow and steady wins the race
The lesson is shown by what happens
teach.note: Ask the class to explain the moral in their own words. Link to Islam: the Prophet (peace be upon him) is reported in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim to have said that the most beloved deeds to Allah are those done regularly, even if small. Keep the link brief and respectful.

practice: Find and copy one word that shows the tortoise moved slowly.
What did the hare do instead of racing?
independent: Answer in full sentences: (a) What did the hare boast? (b) Where was the finish line? (c) Why was the hare late? (d) What is the moral?
Draw a story map with four boxes: boast, race, nap, finish.
List three features of a fable using the story as evidence.
exit: Write the moral of the fable.
Who is the main character who makes a mistake?
lessons.homework: Retell the fable to a family member and write the moral on a card.
lessons.send: SEND: read the story with a partner; give picture sequencing cards. EAL: pre-teach boasted, plodded, sprinted. Stretch: suggest another moral and defend it.

lessons.title: Characters and inference
objectives: Use evidence from the text to say what a character is like
Explain the meaning of words in context

keywords.def: work out something that the author does not say directly
words from the text that prove your idea

starter: What is the moral of The Hare and the Tortoise?
Find the verb: The tortoise plodded on.

teach.heading: Inference
bullets: Authors do not tell us everything
We use clues to work it out
I think... because the text says...
teach.note: Show a picture of a child holding an umbrella and ask what the weather is. Explain that we use clues. Reading is detective work: we find evidence in the text to support our ideas.

teach.heading: What was the hare like?
bullets: He thought he had plenty of time: overconfident
teach.note: Reread the fable and underline clues about the hare. Model a full answer: 'I think the hare was proud because he said he could win with his eyes closed.' Ask pupils to find another.

teach.heading: What was the tortoise like?
bullets: He plodded on and never stopped: determined
teach.note: Contrast the tortoise's quiet reply with the hare's boast. Ask which character we should copy. Link to humility as a value we admire in Islam, without making false claims about texts.

teach.heading: Words in context
teach.note: Show how neighbouring words help with meaning: 'plodded on, step by step'. Ask pupils to replace each word with a simpler one and check it still makes sense.

teach.heading: Write an inference answer
bullets: Evidence: he lay down for a nap
Explain: he forgot the race was still going
teach.note: Model a P.E.E. style answer: Point, Evidence, Explain. Keep it simple for Year 3. Ask for sentence starters: 'This shows that...'

practice: How do you know the tortoise was determined?
Which word shows how the hare ran at the end?

independent: Write two sentences about the hare using 'I think... because...' with a quotation.
Write two sentences about the tortoise in the same way.
Choose a new adjective for each character and prove it with evidence.
exit: Complete: I think the hare was careless because...
lessons.homework: Write a character description of the hare using three adjectives and evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and highlighted evidence. EAL: act the words boasted and plodded. Stretch: compare how the hare feels at the start and end.

teach.note: Write live.

steps: Topic sentence: Airports across Europe closed for about six days.
Fact: Around 100,000 flights were cancelled.
Quotation: "We waited for five days to fly home," said one traveller (an imagined eyewitness).
Close: Flights began again once the ash cleared.
model.answer: A formal paragraph with a quotation

teach.heading: Hinge: punctuation
teach.note: Teams poll.

check.q: Which quotation is punctuated correctly?
options: "The ash looked like snow," said a farmer.
"The ash looked like snow" said a farmer.
The ash looked like snow, said a farmer.
check.why: The spoken words and the comma sit inside the inverted commas.

bullets: Write on your own from your plan
teach.note: Note any support given; judge against the Year 3 writing criteria.

practice.q: Write your headline
practice.a: For example: ASH CLOUD STOPS EUROPE'S FLIGHTS

independent.q: Core: write your report: headline, opening paragraph, two more paragraphs and a quotation
independent.a: A complete newspaper report

independent.q: Extend: add a sub-heading above paragraphs 2 and 3
independent.a: Two sub-headings

lessons.title: Proofreading and publishing the report: headline, sub-headings and layout

objectives: To understand how to proofread a report and publish it with a clear newspaper layout
successCriteria: All: proofread for three kinds of error
Most: improve the headline with alliteration
Some: lay out the report in columns with a caption

words close together starting with the same sound: Ash Attack
a narrow block of text on a newspaper page
a short line under a picture

hook.a: The second: alliteration and a powerful verb grab attention.

lessons.title: I am the volcano: a personified narrative and our year of writing
lessons.bigQuestion: What would a volcano say if it could tell its own story?
objectives: To understand how to write a short first-person narrative using personification
successCriteria: All: write in the first person as the volcano
Most: use personification and powerful verbs
Some: read it aloud and reflect on my year of writing

keywords.def: describing a thing as if it were alive
writing as I and me
a precise action word: roared, slept, stirred
think back on what we have learned

hook.text: If you were a volcano, what would you be thinking just before you woke?
hook.a: I have slept for so long; something is stirring deep inside me...

pictures.alt: steam rising from a volcanic vent

resources: Tarbiyyah Primary English scheme of work, Tremors: Express (a short narrative from the point of view of a natural disaster; first person; read expressively)
Personification planning sheet (pupil PDF)
Pupil's writing from this year (exercise book) for reflection
Mini-whiteboard and pen

starter.q: Change to first person: The volcano slept.
Give a powerful verb for a volcano

teach.heading: Model: I am the volcano
teach.note: Write live; label techniques.

steps: First person: For a thousand years, I slept beneath my coat of snow.
Personification: My stony heart began to stir.
Powerful verbs: I yawned, and grey breath rose into the sky.
Ending: Then I settled again, quiet and watchful, as the land turned green.
model.answer: A personified first-person narrative

teach.heading: Hinge: first person
teach.note: Teams poll.

check.q: Which sentence is in the first person?
check.why: I shows the volcano is telling its own story.

teach.note: Choose two.

teach.heading: Our year of writing
bullets: Look back at your first piece in January
Find your best piece this year
Name one thing you do better now
teach.note: Celebrate progress.

practice.q: Write a first-person personified sentence
practice.a: For example: I stretched my rocky arms towards the sky.
practice.model: I do: I (first person) + a human action (stretched my arms) for a volcano.

independent.q: Core: write a short first-person narrative as a volcano with personification
independent.a: A short narrative in the first person

independent.q: Extend: read your narrative aloud with expression
independent.a: An expressive reading

independent.a: For example: In January I wrote short sentences. Now I use fronted adverbials and paragraphs.
